hi-china.title: hi-china.summary
Imperial China: Dynasties, inventions and exams across more than 3,000 years.

hi-china.title: hi-china.q0.x
Imperial China: He took the new title "First Emperor".

hi-china.title: hi-china.q1.q
Imperial China: What were Shang oracle bones used for?

hi-china.title: hi-china.q1.x
Imperial China: Diviners heated them and read the cracks.

hi-china.title: hi-china.q2.q
Imperial China: Which dynasty built most of the stone and brick Great Wall seen today?

hi-china.title: hi-china.q3.q
Imperial China: Which is NOT one of China's four great inventions?

hi-china.title: hi-china.q3.x
Imperial China: The four are paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder.

hi-china.title: hi-china.q4.q
Imperial China: When did the last emperor, Puyi, abdicate?

hi-china.title: hi-china.q4.x
Imperial China: The Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 January 1912.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c0.text
Imperial China: China's oldest writing survives on bones. Around 1200 BCE, kings of the Shang dynasty asked their ancestors about harvests, wars and illness by heating ox shoulder blades and turtle shells until they cracked.\n\nDiviners read the cracks and carved the question, and sometimes the result, into the bone. Those signs are the direct ancestors of today's Chinese characters.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c1.text
Imperial China: After centuries of war between rival states, King Zheng of Qin conquered them all and in 221 BCE declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the "First Emperor".\n\nHe ruled through appointed officials rather than nobles, and imposed one script, one currency and one system of weights. His dynasty collapsed soon after his death, but the idea of a single China lasted.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c2.text
Imperial China: The Great Wall is not one wall but many, built over about 2,000 years by different states and dynasties to guard farmland against horsemen from the northern steppe.\n\nThe famous stone and brick sections near Beijing are fairly recent: most were built by the Ming dynasty, mainly in the 1500s. Older walls were mostly made of rammed earth.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c3.title
Imperial China: The Han and the Silk Road

hi-china.title: hi-china.c3.text
Imperial China: The Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) ruled about as many people as the Roman Empire, at the same time. Most Chinese people still call themselves Han.\n\nHan armies and envoys opened routes through Central Asia. Along them, silk travelled west, while horses, new crops and, later, Buddhism came east.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c4.text
Imperial China: For about 1,300 years, from 605 to 1905, China chose many of its officials through written exams on the Confucian classics, rather than by birth alone.\n\nCandidates memorised hundreds of thousands of characters of ancient text and wrote essays on how to govern. Passing brought prestige, power and wealth to a whole family.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c5.text
Imperial China: Paper, printing, the magnetic compass and gunpowder are often called China's "four great inventions". Each one later spread west and changed the world.\n\nIn 1620 the English philosopher Francis Bacon wrote that printing, gunpowder and the compass had transformed the world more than any empire. He did not know where they came from.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c6.text
Imperial China: The Tang dynasty (618–907) ruled from Chang'an, perhaps the world's largest city, full of merchants, monks and envoys from across Asia. It was the golden age of Chinese poetry.\n\nThe Song (960–1279) was weaker militarily but richer: rice farming boomed, cities grew, and the government issued the world's first paper money.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c7.text
Imperial China: Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven huge fleets across the Indian Ocean, reaching India, Arabia and East Africa.\n\nThe voyages showed off Ming power and collected tribute. Then they stopped: the court turned inward, and China left the oceans to others, decades before the Portuguese arrived.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c8.text
Imperial China: In 1644 the Manchus, from the north-east, took Beijing and founded the Qing, China's last dynasty. Under emperors such as Kangxi and Qianlong it nearly doubled in size and grew rich.\n\nIn the 1800s it faced rising Western powers, two Opium Wars, unequal treaties and a devastating civil war, the Taiping Rebellion.

hi-china.title: hi-china.c9.text
Imperial China: After defeats by Western powers and by Japan, reforms came too late. In October 1911 an army uprising in Wuchang spread across the provinces.\n\nOn 1 January 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed, and in February the six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicated. More than 2,000 years of imperial rule, begun by the First Emperor in 221 BCE, were over.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.summary
Imperial China: How steppe horsemen built the largest land empire in history, and what it left behind.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q0.q
Imperial China: In which year was Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan?

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q0.x
Imperial China: A great assembly, the kurultai, gave him the title.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q1.x
Imperial China: Riders changed horses at stations across the empire.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q2.q
Imperial China: Which city did Kublai Khan build as his capital?

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q2.x
Imperial China: Beijing has been China's capital for most of the time since.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q3.q
Imperial China: Where did the Black Death probably begin?

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.q3.x
Imperial China: DNA from 1338–39 graves in Kyrgyzstan points there.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c0.text
Imperial China: Temüjin was born around 1162 on the Mongolian steppe. After his father was poisoned, his family was abandoned and lived in poverty, hunting marmots and gathering roots.\n\nThrough alliances, loyalty and war he united the feuding steppe tribes. In 1206 a great assembly proclaimed him Genghis Khan, ruler of all the "people of the felt tents".

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c1.text
Imperial China: The Mongol army was made of mounted archers. Each rider carried a powerful composite bow and could shoot accurately at a gallop, standing in the stirrups.\n\nEach warrior had several horses and changed mounts to keep them fresh. Fast, disciplined units could encircle an enemy, retreat on purpose to draw it into a trap, and wheel round again.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c1.viz.items.0
Imperial China: Composite bow of horn and wood

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c2.text
Imperial China: Mongol armies carried little and lived off their animals and the land. Riders had dried milk curd, dried meat and fermented mare's milk, and herds travelled with them.\n\nWithout slow supply wagons they could move much faster than their enemies, cross deserts and mountains, and appear where nobody expected them.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c3.text
Imperial China: At its peak, around 1270, the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to Hungary and from Siberia to the Persian Gulf, about 24 million km².\n\nIt is the largest continuous land empire in history. Only the British Empire, spread across oceans, was larger in total. Yet the Mongols themselves may have numbered only about a million people.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c4.text
Imperial China: To rule such distances, the Mongols built the yam, a network of relay stations across the empire, with fresh horses, food and lodging for official riders.\n\nMessengers carrying a metal tablet called a paiza could change horses at each station and ride on day and night, carrying news far faster than ever before.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c5.text
Imperial China: Once the conquests settled, the Mongols ruled most of the Silk Road routes themselves. For about a century, roughly 1250 to 1350, merchants and travellers could cross Eurasia under one political umbrella.\n\nHistorians call this the Pax Mongolica, the "Mongol peace". Goods, ideas, technologies and people moved between China, Persia and Europe as never before.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c6.text
Imperial China: Kublai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became Great Khan in 1260 and founded the Yuan dynasty in China in 1271. By 1279 he had conquered the Song, the first non-Chinese ruler of all China.\n\nHis capital, Dadu, grew into today's Beijing. He ruled through a mix of Mongol, Central Asian and Chinese officials and used paper money across the empire.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c7.text
Imperial China: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo travelled to Kublai Khan's court with his father and uncle, stayed about 17 years and returned to Venice in 1295.\n\nLater, as a prisoner of war in Genoa, he dictated his story to a writer of romances. *The Description of the World* amazed Europe with tales of paper money, huge cities and stones that burned.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c8.text
Imperial China: The Black Death probably began in Central Asia in the 1330s. The same Mongol-era trade routes that carried silk and spices helped carry the plague bacterium west.\n\nBy 1346 it had reached the Black Sea, where Italian merchants traded with the Mongol Golden Horde. Their ships then brought it to the Mediterranean.

hi-china.title: hi-mongols.c9.text
Imperial China: After 1260 the empire split into four khanates ruled by different branches of Genghis Khan's family, often at war with each other.\n\nThey gradually broke up or were absorbed, but the Mongols left a deep mark: on Russia, China and Iran, on trade between East and West, and on the very idea of a world connected from end to end.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.summary
Imperial China: Three great civilisations of the Americas, their cities, science and crops, and the conquest that ended their independence.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q0.q
Imperial China: Which civilisation invented a Long Count calendar with a zero?

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q0.x
Imperial China: Their dates counted days from 3114 BCE.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q1.o1
Imperial China: Farm plots built up in a lake

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q2.q
Imperial China: What did the Inca use quipus for?

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q2.x
Imperial China: Knots in set positions stood for numbers.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q3.q
Imperial China: Which factor killed most indigenous people after the conquest?

hi-china.title: hi-americas.q3.x
Imperial China: They had no immunity to Old World diseases.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c0.text
Imperial China: The civilisations of the Americas grew from crops domesticated there thousands of years earlier. Maize came from a wild grass in Mexico; potatoes from the high Andes.\n\nThese plants fed cities, armies and priests, just as wheat and rice did in Eurasia. Today maize and potatoes are among the most important foods on Earth.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c1.text
Imperial China: The Maya built hundreds of cities in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras, with stepped pyramids, palaces, plazas and ball courts.\n\nThey were never one empire. Rival city-states such as Tikal and Calakmul, each ruled by a divine king, fought and allied with each other for centuries.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c2.text
Imperial China: The Maya developed the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, with signs for whole words and signs for syllables.\n\nThey carved it on stone monuments, painted it on pottery and wrote books on bark paper. After years of work, scholars can now read most surviving texts: they record kings, wars, births and rituals.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c3.text
Imperial China: Maya numbers used just three signs: a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero. They counted in twenties, not tens.\n\nWith them they kept several calendars, including the Long Count, which numbered days from a starting point in 3114 BCE. It needed a true zero, which the Maya invented independently of India.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c4.text
Imperial China: The Mexica, better known as the Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. By 1519 it may have had over 200,000 people, larger than any city in Spain.\n\nIt was fed by chinampas: narrow fields built up from lake mud, separated by canals. They could give several harvests a year.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c5.text
Imperial China: The Inca Empire, ruled from Cusco, was the largest in the Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile. A road network of about 30,000 km held it together.\n\nThe Inca had no wheeled transport and no horses. Roads carried people on foot, llama caravans and relay runners who passed messages from station to station.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c6.text
Imperial China: The Inca had no writing in the usual sense. Officials kept records with quipus: bundles of coloured strings tied with knots.\n\nThe position and type of each knot stood for a number, in a base-ten system. Quipus recorded censuses, taxes and storehouse contents across the empire. Whether some also recorded words is still debated.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c7.text
Imperial China: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, on a ridge high above the Urubamba river in Peru.\n\nThe Spanish never found it. It became world famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham visited in 1911, guided by local farmers who already knew it well.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c8.text
Imperial China: Small Spanish forces conquered the Aztec and Inca empires within a few years: Hernán Cortés took Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532.\n\nSteel, horses and guns helped, but two things mattered more: thousands of indigenous allies who hated Aztec or Inca rule, and new diseases such as smallpox, which killed vast numbers.

hi-china.title: hi-americas.c9.text
Imperial China: The empires fell, but their peoples did not vanish. Millions still speak Quechua, Maya languages and Nahuatl, and indigenous traditions shape life from Mexico to Bolivia.\n\nThe rest of the world inherited their crops, from maize, potatoes and tomatoes to chillies, cacao and vanilla, and words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and llama.
